It does not provide individualized health guidance or replace professional care. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have a health condition, or take any medications, talk to a qualified healthcare professional before starting, stopping, or combining supplements.

tips.title: Vitamin D: take with a meal that includes fat
tips.coverText: Vitamin D is fat-soluble. Take it with a meal that contains some fat.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin often taken for bone and overall health.

**Why it matters**
- Fat-soluble nutrients are generally absorbed better with dietary fat than on an empty stomach.

**How to use safely**
- If you supplement, consider taking vitamin D with a meal (not necessarily a large one) that includes some fat.

**Watch-outs**
- If you take multiple supplements, watch for duplicated vitamin D across products.
- Talk to a healthcare professional if you have kidney disease, hypercalcemia, or take prescription medicines.

**Sources**
- [Vitamin D - Consumer Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminD-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)
- [Dietary Supplements: What You Need to Know (Consumer Fact Sheet)](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/WYNTK-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

**Disclaimer**

tips.title: Vitamin D: more isn’t always better
tips.coverText: High-dose vitamin D can be harmful. Avoid mega-doses unless a clinician advises it.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium.

**Why it matters**
- Very high intakes can raise calcium levels and may cause harm over time.

**How to use safely**
- Use the label to see how much vitamin D you’re taking per day (and add up across products).

**Watch-outs**
- If you have kidney disease, hyperparathyroidism, or a history of kidney stones, talk to a healthcare professional before supplementing.
- Ask a clinician about blood testing if you’re considering higher-dose use.

**Sources**
- [Vitamin D - Consumer Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminD-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

tips.title: Vitamin D2 vs D3: check the form on the label
tips.coverText: Vitamin D comes as D2 or D3. If you compare products, note the form and dose.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Vitamin D supplements typically contain vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol) or D3 (cholecalciferol).

**Why it matters**
- Different forms can have different potency in the body, so comparing “dose” works best when you also note the form.

**How to use safely**
- When switching brands, keep the same daily amount unless your clinician recommends a change—and note D2 vs D3.

**Watch-outs**
- If you’re on a prescribed vitamin D regimen, don’t swap products without checking with your prescriber.

**Sources**

tips.title: Calcium: split larger daily amounts
tips.coverText: Calcium absorption may be better in smaller doses. If taking more, consider splitting across meals.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Calcium is a mineral best known for supporting bones and teeth.

**Why it matters**
- Your body absorbs calcium in limited amounts at a time; splitting can improve tolerance and may improve absorption.

**How to use safely**
- If your label suggests multiple tablets, taking them at different times of day (e.g., with meals) may be easier on the stomach.

**Watch-outs**
- If you have kidney stones or kidney disease, talk to a healthcare professional before using calcium supplements.
- Check if your multivitamin already includes calcium.

**Sources**
- [Calcium - Consumer Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Calcium-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

**Disclaimer**
- General education only. Not medical advice.

tips.title: Calcium carbonate vs citrate: timing differs
tips.coverText: Take calcium carbonate with food for better absorption. Calcium citrate can be taken with or without food.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Calcium supplements commonly use calcium carbonate or calcium citrate.

**Why it matters**
- The form can affect how well calcium is absorbed and how the product feels in your stomach.

**How to use safely**
- If a product uses calcium carbonate, taking it with food may improve absorption; calcium citrate is often absorbed well with or without food.

**Watch-outs**
- If you take acid-reducing medicines, ask a clinician/pharmacist which form is a better fit.
- Talk to a healthcare professional if you have kidney disease or a history of kidney stones.

**Sources**
- [Calcium - Consumer Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Calcium-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)
- [The Scoop - February 2011 (Calcium carbonate vs citrate and timing)](https://ods.od.nih.gov/News/The_Scoop_-_February_2011.aspx) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

**Disclaimer**

tips.title: Calcium can bind some medicines
tips.coverText: Calcium can interfere with absorption of some meds. Separate from thyroid meds/iron when advised.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Calcium can bind to certain medications in the gut, reducing how much your body absorbs.

**Why it matters**
- Spacing supplements from certain prescriptions can help avoid unintended “lower dosing” of your medication.

**How to use safely**
- If you take thyroid hormone or iron, ask your pharmacist about spacing calcium away from those meds.

**Watch-outs**
- If you take prescription medicines, ask a healthcare professional before starting calcium supplements.
- High total calcium intake (food + supplements) may not be appropriate for everyone.
- Talk to a healthcare professional before use if you take medications or have a medical condition.

**Sources**

tips.title: Magnesium: the UL applies to supplements
tips.coverText: Magnesium UL applies to supplements/meds, not food. Add totals from supplements, antacids, laxatives.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Magnesium is an essential mineral; it’s also used in some antacids and laxatives.

**Why it matters**
- Excess magnesium from supplements/medications can cause side effects (often GI-related), especially at higher amounts.

**How to use safely**
- Add up magnesium from all supplements and products (including antacids/laxatives) to avoid unintentionally high totals.

**Watch-outs**
- People with kidney disease should talk to a healthcare professional before using magnesium supplements.
- If magnesium causes diarrhea, consider lowering the amount or switching products—with clinician guidance if needed.

**Sources**
- [Magnesium - Consumer Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Magnesium-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)
- [Magnesium Fact Sheet for Consumers (PDF)](https://ods.od.nih.gov/pdf/factsheets/magnesium-consumer.pdf) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

**Disclaimer**
- General education only. Not medical advice.

tips.title: Magnesium forms: tolerability can differ
tips.coverText: Magnesium forms vary in tolerance/absorption. If one causes diarrhea, try another form or a lower dose.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Supplement labels may list magnesium as citrate, chloride, oxide, glycinate, etc.

**Why it matters**
- Different forms can vary in absorption and GI tolerance; labels may also differ in ‘elemental magnesium’ per serving.

**How to use safely**
- If one product upsets your stomach, another form (or a lower amount) may be better tolerated.

**Watch-outs**
- Don’t assume ‘more mg’ is better—compare the *elemental* magnesium amount.
- Talk to a healthcare professional if you have kidney disease or take prescription medicines.

**Sources**
- [Magnesium Fact Sheet for Consumers (PDF)](https://ods.od.nih.gov/pdf/factsheets/magnesium-consumer.pdf) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)
- [Magnesium - Consumer Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Magnesium-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

tips.title: Magnesium: try taking with food for GI comfort
tips.coverText: Magnesium can upset your stomach on an empty stomach. Try taking it with food (if the label allows).
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Magnesium supplements are used for many reasons, but GI side effects are common.

**Why it matters**
- Taking supplements with food can reduce nausea or stomach discomfort for some people.

**How to use safely**
- If your product allows, try taking magnesium with a meal and track how you feel for a week.

**Watch-outs**
- If you use magnesium as a laxative or antacid, the timing may be different—follow the label or clinician advice.
- Talk to a healthcare professional if you have kidney disease.

**Sources**

tips.title: Iron: supplement only when it’s needed
tips.coverText: Iron is essential—but too much can be harmful. Don’t start iron unless a clinician suggests it.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Iron helps your body make hemoglobin to carry oxygen in blood.

**Why it matters**
- Unlike many nutrients, excess iron can be risky—so it’s a supplement where “need” matters.

**How to use safely**
- If you think you’re low, ask a healthcare professional about testing and whether supplementation makes sense.

**Watch-outs**
- Keep iron supplements away from children—accidental ingestion can be dangerous.
- If you have hemochromatosis or other iron-overload conditions, avoid iron supplements unless supervised.
- Talk to a healthcare professional before use if you take medications or have a medical condition.

**Sources**
- [Iron - Consumer Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)
- [Iron Fact Sheet for Consumers (PDF)](https://ods.od.nih.gov/pdf/factsheets/iron-consumer.pdf) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

tips.title: Iron: vitamin C can help absorption
tips.coverText: Non-heme iron absorbs better with vitamin C foods. Pair with citrus, peppers, or tomatoes.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Iron from plant sources (non-heme) is less readily absorbed than heme iron from animal foods.

**Why it matters**
- Vitamin C–rich foods can help your body absorb non-heme iron.

**How to use safely**
- If you take iron or eat iron-fortified foods, consider pairing with vitamin C–rich foods.

**Watch-outs**
- Some people get stomach upset from iron; following the label and taking with food may help.
- If you take prescription medicines, ask a pharmacist about spacing and interactions.

**Sources**
- [Iron Fact Sheet for Consumers (PDF)](https://ods.od.nih.gov/pdf/factsheets/iron-consumer.pdf) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

tips.title: Iron: watch timing with calcium/coffee
tips.coverText: Some foods/supplements can reduce iron absorption. If needed, take iron away from calcium/coffee.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Iron absorption can be affected by what you take it with.

**Why it matters**
- Spacing can help ensure you actually absorb what’s on the label.

**How to use safely**
- If you use both calcium and iron supplements, ask a pharmacist about spacing them; the same can apply to coffee/tea for some people.

**Watch-outs**
- If you are pregnant, have anemia, or take multiple medications, talk to a healthcare professional for individualized guidance.

tips.title: Zinc: long-term high doses can backfire
tips.coverText: High zinc over time can lower copper levels. Avoid long-term mega-doses; check your total intake.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Zinc is an essential mineral involved in immune function and wound healing.

**Why it matters**
- Taking too much zinc for a long time can reduce copper absorption and may affect immune function.

**How to use safely**
- If you take zinc, total it across products (multis + single zinc) and stick to label directions unless supervised.

**Watch-outs**
- Talk to a healthcare professional if you take zinc long-term, are pregnant/breastfeeding, or take prescription medicines.

**Sources**
- [Zinc - Consumer Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Zinc-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)
- [Dietary Supplements for Immune Function and Infectious Diseases (Consumer Fact Sheet)](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/ImmuneFunction-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

tips.title: Zinc: take with food if it upsets your stomach
tips.coverText: Zinc can cause nausea on an empty stomach. Take it with food (unless the label says otherwise).
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Zinc supplements come in many forms (gluconate, picolinate, etc.).

**Why it matters**
- GI upset is a common reason people stop taking zinc—even if the dose is modest.

**How to use safely**
- If you feel nauseated, try taking zinc with food (unless the label says otherwise).

**Watch-outs**
- High-dose zinc can also cause GI symptoms; more is not always better.
- Talk to a healthcare professional if you take multiple supplements or take medicines.

**Sources**
- [Zinc - Consumer Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Zinc-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

**Disclaimer**

tips.title: Zinc lozenges: don’t exceed the label
tips.coverText: Some people use zinc lozenges for colds. Use short-term and avoid stacking multiple zinc products.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Zinc is sometimes marketed for immune support and cold symptoms.

**Why it matters**
- Short-term use differs from long-term daily use; the same ‘zinc’ may come from tablets, lozenges, and multis.

**How to use safely**
- If you use a zinc lozenge, check the mg per lozenge and the max per day—and pause other zinc supplements.

**Watch-outs**
- If you have ongoing symptoms or take medicines, talk to a healthcare professional.

**Sources**

tips.title: Selenium: know the toxicity signs
tips.coverText: Too much selenium can harm hair and nails. Avoid stacking selenium products—total your daily selenium (mcg).
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Selenium is a trace mineral involved in thyroid hormone metabolism and antioxidant systems.

**Why it matters**
- The margin between ‘enough’ and ‘too much’ can be smaller than people assume.

**How to use safely**
- Check your multivitamin and any single selenium product; avoid doubling up unless advised.

**Watch-outs**
- Potential signs of too much selenium include hair loss or brittle nails—stop and seek medical advice if concerned.
- Talk to a healthcare professional if you have thyroid disease or take prescription medicines.

**Sources**
- [Selenium - Consumer Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Selenium-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

**Disclaimer**
- General education only. Not medical advice.

tips.title: Brazil nuts + selenium: easy to overdo
tips.coverText: Brazil nuts are selenium-dense. If you eat them often, be cautious with selenium supplements and your multi.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Selenium comes from food and supplements; Brazil nuts are a concentrated food source.

**Why it matters**
- It’s possible to exceed safe intakes when high-selenium foods and supplements are combined.

**How to use safely**
- If you regularly eat Brazil nuts, check whether your supplement also contains selenium before adding more.

**Watch-outs**
- If you have thyroid disease or take medications, talk to a healthcare professional.

tips.title: Selenium forms: check what’s on the label
tips.coverText: Selenium may be listed as selenomethionine, yeast, or selenite. Compare products by micrograms per serving.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Supplements can contain selenium in several chemical forms.

**Why it matters**
- Form names vary, but most users should focus on total micrograms (mcg) and avoiding excess.

**How to use safely**
- Compare products by mcg per serving and serving size—then add up across products.

**Watch-outs**
- If a label uses a proprietary blend, you may not see individual selenium amounts—consider a transparent label instead.

tips.title: Iodine: extra isn’t always helpful
tips.coverText: Too little or too much iodine can affect the thyroid. If you have thyroid disease, ask a clinician first.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Iodine is required to make thyroid hormones.

**Why it matters**
- Excess iodine can trigger thyroid problems in susceptible people; ‘more’ is not automatically better.

**How to use safely**
- If you supplement, pick a product with a clear iodine amount (mcg) and avoid combining multiple iodine sources.

**Watch-outs**
- Talk to a healthcare professional if you have thyroid disease or take thyroid medicine.
- Seaweed/kelp supplements can contain high or variable iodine—check the label carefully.

**Sources**
- [Iodine - Consumer Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iodine-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

tips.title: Iodine matters in pregnancy—but don’t self-dose
tips.coverText: Iodine needs are higher in pregnancy. Use a prenatal with disclosed iodine, and confirm with your OB.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Adequate iodine supports fetal brain development via thyroid hormones.

**Why it matters**
- Both deficiency and excess can be problematic; prenatal products vary in iodine content.

**How to use safely**
- If pregnant, check whether your prenatal includes iodine (mcg) and discuss supplementation with your prenatal care team.

**Watch-outs**
- If you have thyroid disease, get individualized guidance before supplementing iodine.
- Talk to a healthcare professional before use if you take medications or have a medical condition.

**Sources**

tips.title: Kelp/sea moss iodine: verify the amount
tips.coverText: Seaweed-based supplements can be very iodine-dense. Prefer products with a measured iodine amount.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Some ‘seaweed’ supplements (e.g., kelp/sea moss) can be major iodine sources.

**Why it matters**
- If iodine isn’t quantified, you can’t manage your intake—especially if you also use iodized salt or a multivitamin.

**How to use safely**
- Choose products that list iodine in micrograms (mcg) per serving and avoid ‘unknown dose’ blends.

**Watch-outs**
- If you have thyroid disease or take thyroid medication, talk to a healthcare professional before using seaweed supplements.

tips.title: Potassium: prioritize food unless told otherwise
tips.coverText: Potassium supplements aren’t for everyone. Food sources are often the safest first step.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Potassium is a mineral needed for normal cell function, including heart and muscle function.

**Why it matters**
- People’s potassium needs and safe limits can vary widely depending on kidney function and medications.

**How to use safely**
- Focus on potassium-rich foods first, and view potassium supplements as something to use with clinician guidance.

**Watch-outs**
- Talk to a healthcare professional before using potassium supplements if you have kidney disease, heart disease, or take blood pressure medicines.

**Sources**

tips.title: Potassium + certain meds: a high-risk combo
tips.coverText: Some medicines raise potassium levels. If you take BP meds or have kidney disease, ask first.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Some prescription medicines can increase potassium in the blood.

**Why it matters**
- Combining those medicines with potassium supplements (or salt substitutes high in potassium) can be risky.

**How to use safely**
- If you take ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, or have kidney disease, get clinician advice before adding potassium.

**Watch-outs**
- Symptoms of high potassium are not always obvious—don’t ‘trial-and-error’ potassium supplements.
- Talk to a healthcare professional before use if you take medications or have a medical condition.

tips.coverText: Supplement Facts can hide totals via serving size. Multiply mg per serving by servings/day.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Potassium amounts are listed in milligrams (mg) on Supplement Facts panels.

**How to use safely**
- Always check ‘Serving Size’ and ‘Servings Per Container,’ and compute the daily total from the directions.

**Watch-outs**

tips.title: Vitamin A: pregnancy is a ‘retinol’ caution zone
tips.coverText: High preformed vitamin A (retinol) can be harmful in pregnancy. Use prenatal guidance; ask your clinician.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Vitamin A includes preformed vitamin A (retinol/retinyl esters) and provitamin A carotenoids (e.g., beta-carotene).

**Why it matters**
- Excess preformed vitamin A can be toxic and is a special concern in pregnancy.

**How to use safely**
- If pregnant (or trying), review your multivitamin/prenatal label for vitamin A form and amount, and confirm with your OB.

**Watch-outs**
- Avoid stacking multiple ‘vitamin A’ products unless supervised.
- If you have liver disease or take prescription retinoids, talk to a healthcare professional before using vitamin A supplements.

**Sources**

tips.title: Vitamin B6: high doses can damage nerves
tips.coverText: Too much vitamin B6 over time can cause nerve problems. Avoid high-dose B6 unless supervised.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Vitamin B6 (often as pyridoxine) is involved in many enzyme reactions.

**Why it matters**
- Long-term high-dose vitamin B6 supplementation has been linked to nerve damage (neuropathy) in some people.

**How to use safely**
- Check whether your multivitamin or ‘B-complex’ already includes B6 before adding a separate B6 product.

**Watch-outs**
- If you notice tingling, numbness, or burning sensations, stop the product and seek medical advice.
- Talk to a healthcare professional if you’re considering high-dose B6.

**Why it matters**

**How to use safely**

- If you use multiple products daily, consider simplifying to one base supplement and reassessing.

tips.title: %DV: a fast way to judge ‘how much’
tips.coverText: Daily Value (%DV) rules vary by country. Use %DV to compare products and spot high-dose formulas.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- % Daily Value (%DV) shows how much a nutrient in one serving contributes to a daily reference intake on that label.

**Why it matters**
- %DV helps you compare products quickly and identify high-dose formulas.

**How to use safely**
- DV conventions differ by country and label type.
- Some labels use rules of thumb (e.g., in the U.S., ≤5% DV is low and ≥20% DV is high).
- In Canada’s Nutrition Facts table, ≤5% DV is “a little” and ≥15% DV is “a lot.”
- When %DV isn’t shown, compare the absolute amount per serving and the serving size.
- When in doubt, check your local health authority’s guidance for how %DV is defined on your label.

**Watch-outs**
- If you’re pregnant, have chronic disease, or take medicines, talk to a healthcare professional before high-dose supplements.

**What it is**
- Many supplement labels use structure/function-style claims (e.g., “supports immune health”).

**Why it matters**
- These claims describe support of normal body function. They are not the same as strong clinical proof, and they don’t mean a product is authorized for a disease benefit.

**How to use safely**
- Use claims as a starting point, then check the ingredient, the dose, and the evidence.
- Look for any legal disclaimers or license/registration identifiers used in your market.
- When comparing products, prioritize clear labeling over vague promises.

**Watch-outs**
- If a label claims it can “get rid of” a disease, replace a prescription, or promises dramatic results, that’s a red flag—talk to a healthcare professional.

**Sources**
- [Structure/Function Claims](https://www.fda.gov/food/nutrition-food-labeling-and-critical-foods/structurefunction-claims) — U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
- [Licensed Natural Health Products Database (LNHPD)](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/drugs-health-products/natural-non-prescription/applications-submissions/product-licensing/licensed-natural-health-products-database.html) — Health Canada
- [Labelling of natural health products (guidance)](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/drugs-health-products/natural-non-prescription/legislation-guidelines/guidance-documents/labelling.html) — Health Canada
- [Dietary Supplements: What You Need to Know (Consumer Fact Sheet)](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/WYNTK-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

**Disclaimer**
- General education only. Not medical advice.

tips.title: If a supplement harms you: report it
tips.coverText: Stop the product and get help for serious reactions. You can also report it to your local health authority.
tips.detailMarkdown:
**What it is**
- Side effects and adverse reactions can happen from contamination, interactions, or excessive dosing.

**Why it matters**
- Reporting helps health authorities identify unsafe products and protect other consumers.

**How to use safely**
- Stop the product if you suspect a reaction.
- For serious symptoms, seek urgent medical care.
- Report the event through your local regulator’s reporting system.

**Watch-outs**
- Keep the bottle/label (or photos) and note the brand, lot number, dose, and when symptoms started.
- Talk to a healthcare professional before using supplements if you take medications or have a medical condition.

**Sources**
- [How to Report a Problem with Dietary Supplements](https://www.fda.gov/food/dietary-supplements/how-report-problem-dietary-supplements) — U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
- [Report a side effect of a health product](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/drugs-health-products/medeffect-canada/adverse-reaction-reporting.html) — Health Canada
- [Dietary Supplements: What You Need to Know (Consumer Fact Sheet)](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/WYNTK-Consumer/) — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)

**Disclaimer**
- General education only. Not medical advice.

rotationAdvanced.notes: Optional client-side cadence to avoid back-to-back high-warning tips while remaining offline-deterministic and preserving the tips array order. Pattern includes each pillar at least once per week, with safety twice.
rotationAdvanced.selectionFormula:
1) days = daysSinceEpoch(localDate)
2) slot = days % 7
3) bucket = cadencePattern7Days[slot].pillarKey
4) k = occurrencesOf(bucket in cadencePattern7Days before slot) + floor(days/7) * occurrencesPerWeek(bucket)
5) baseIndex = k % bucketList.length
6) tip = bucketList[baseIndex]
7) Optional guard: if tip.riskLevel == 'high' AND yesterdayTip.riskLevel == 'high', scan forward in bucketList to the next tip with riskLevel != 'high' (wrap around).
